sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: The chapter adopts the standardized terminology of AASHTO Task Force 27 (1990) and PTI (1996) and presents ground anchor materials, anchored system construction and applications.
sections.body: The AASHTO Task Force 27 (1990) and PTI (1996) documents introduced standardized terminology and definitions of ground anchor components, which are adopted throughout the document. The chapter presents ground anchor materials, anchored system construction and anchored system applications. (p. 4)
key_points: Terminology of AASHTO Task Force 27 (1990) and PTI (1996) adopted (p. 4).
Covers anchor materials, anchored system construction and applications (p. 4).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: A prestressed grouted ground anchor (tieback) transmits tension into soil or rock through anchorage, unbonded (free stressing) length and bond length (Figures 1 to 3). The tendon is the prestressing steel, corrosion protection, sheaths, centralizers and spacers, excluding grout and (here, unlike PTI) the anchorage.
sections.body: A prestressed grouted ground anchor is a structural element installed in soil or rock that transmits an applied tensile load into the ground; grouted ground anchors, referred to simply as ground anchors or as "tiebacks", are installed in grout filled drill holes. Basic components are (1) the anchorage, (2) the free stressing (unbonded) length and (3) the bond length (Figure 1). The anchorage, the anchor head, bearing plate and trumpet, transmits the prestressing force from the prestressing steel (bar or strand) to the ground surface or the supported structure (p. 5; Figures 2 and 3 for bar and strand tendons). The unbonded length is the part of the prestressing steel free to elongate elastically and transfer the resisting force from the bond length to the structure; a bondbreaker, a smooth plastic sleeve over the tendon there, prevents bonding to the grout, allowing unobstructed elongation during testing and stressing and leaving the steel unbonded after lock-off. The tendon bond length is the length of prestressing steel bonded to the grout and transmitting the load into the ground; the anchor bond length should be behind the critical failure surface. The tendon includes the prestressing steel (strands or bars), corrosion protection, sheaths (sheathings), centralizers and spacers, and excludes the grout; PTI (1996) also includes the anchorage, but here the tendon is assumed not to. The sheath is a smooth or corrugated pipe or tube protecting the unbonded prestressing steel from corrosion; centralizers position the tendon for the specified minimum grout cover; spacers separate the elements of multiple element tendons so each is bonded to the grout. The grout is a Portland cement based mixture that transfers load from tendon to ground and protects the tendon from corrosion. (pp. 4 to 6)
key_points: Components: anchorage, unbonded (free stressing) length, bond length (Figure 1) (p. 4).
Anchorage = anchor head, bearing plate and trumpet (Figures 2, 3) (p. 4).
Bondbreaker sleeve keeps the unbonded length free to elongate (p. 5).
Anchor bond length located behind the critical failure surface (p. 5).
Tendon excludes grout and, here, the anchorage (unlike PTI 1996) (p. 5).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Three main U.S. types: straight shaft gravity-grouted (Type A), straight shaft pressure-grouted (Type B) and post-grouted (Type C); underreamed (Type D) is uncommon (Figure 4). The contractor usually selects drilling, within engineer limits that protect nearby structures from ground loss and heave.
sections.body: Three main ground anchor types are used in U.S. practice: (1) straight shaft gravity-grouted ground anchors (Type A); (2) straight shaft pressure-grouted ground anchors (Type B); and (3) post-grouted ground anchors (Type C). The underreamed anchor (Type D) is not commonly used today. The types are shown in Figure 4 (p. 7). Drilling methods include rotary, percussion, rotary/percussive or auger drilling (Bruce, 1989). Drilling procedures are usually selected by the contractor, but site conditions may lead the engineer to limit the method, which must not harm structures near the anchors or on the surface; excessive ground loss into the hole and surface heave are the primary causes of such damage. Large diameter hollow stem augered anchors should be discouraged in sands and gravels, since the auger tends to remove more soil than its net volume, possibly losing support of the hole. Drill casing is used in unstable soil or rock, with water or air flushing the cuttings; air flushing needs caution, as excess air pressure may remove groundwater and fines, leading to hole collapse, or cause ground heave (p. 7). (pp. 6 to 7)
key_points: Types A (gravity-grouted), B (pressure-grouted), C (post-grouted); D (underreamed) uncommon (Figure 4) (p. 6).

sections.title: Straight Shaft Gravity-Grouted Ground Anchors
sections.summary: Gravity-grouted straight shaft anchors suit rock and very stiff to hard cohesive soils, drilled by rotary or hollow-stem auger and tremie grouted, cased or uncased; pullout resistance is shear at the grout/ground interface.
sections.body: Straight shaft gravity-grouted ground anchors are typically installed in rock and very stiff to hard cohesive soil deposits using rotary drilling or hollow-stem auger methods, and grouted in the straight borehole by tremie (gravity displacement) methods. The borehole may be cased or uncased depending on its stability. Pullout resistance depends on the shear resistance mobilized at the grout/ground interface. (p. 7)
key_points: For rock and very stiff to hard cohesive soils (p. 7).
Rotary or hollow-stem auger drilling; tremie grouted (p. 7).
Resistance from shear at the grout/ground interface (p. 7).
sections.applicability: Selection among straight shaft gravity-grouted, pressure-grouted, post-grouted and underreamed ground anchors

sections.title: Straight Shaft Pressure-Grouted Ground Anchors
sections.summary: Pressure-grouted straight shaft anchors suit coarse granular soils and weak fissured rock, also fine grained cohesionless soils; grout is injected above 0.35 MPa as auger or casing is withdrawn, raising normal stress on the grout bulb and its effective diameter.
sections.body: Straight shaft pressure-grouted ground anchors are most suitable for coarse granular soils and weak fissured rock, and are also used in fine grained cohesionless soils. Grout is injected into the bond zone at pressures greater than 0.35 MPa; the hole is typically drilled with a hollow stem auger or rotary techniques with casing, and grout is injected under pressure as the auger or casing is withdrawn until the whole anchor bond length is grouted. Compared with tremie grouting this increases pullout resistance by (1) increasing the normal stress (confining pressure) on the grout bulb through local compaction of the surrounding material and (2) increasing the effective diameter of the grout bulb. (p. 8)
key_points: For coarse granular soils, weak fissured rock and fine grained cohesionless soils (p. 8).
Grout injected at more than 0.35 MPa during withdrawal (p. 8).
Higher normal stress and larger effective bulb diameter than tremie grouting (p. 8).

sections.title: Post-grouted Ground Anchors
sections.summary: Post-grouted anchors enlarge gravity grouted bodies by delayed injections, one or two days apart, through a sealed tube with check valves; high pressure grout fractures the set grout and wedges it outward. Systems use a packer per valve or pump without valve control.
sections.body: Post-grouted ground anchors use delayed multiple grout injections, each separated by one or two days, to enlarge the grout body of straight shafted gravity grouted anchors. Postgrouting is through a sealed grout tube installed with the tendon, with check valves in the bond zone that allow additional grout to be injected at high pressure into the set initial grout, fracturing it and wedging it outward into the soil to enlarge the grout body. One system uses a packer to isolate each valve; the other pumps grout down the post-grout tube without controlling which valves open. (p. 8)
key_points: Delayed multiple injections one or two days apart (p. 8).
Sealed grout tube with check valves in the bond zone (p. 8).
Packer-isolated valves or uncontrolled pumping (p. 8).
sections.applicability: Selection among straight shaft gravity-grouted, pressure-grouted, post-grouted and underreamed ground anchors

sections.title: Underreamed Anchors
sections.summary: Underreamed anchors are tremie grouted holes with enlargement bells for firm to hard cohesive deposits; they add end bearing to side shear, but the underreams must be formed and cleaned carefully.
sections.body: Underreamed anchors consist of tremie grouted boreholes with a series of enlargement bells or underreams, usable in firm to hard cohesive deposits. Besides side shear, the principal load transfer mechanism of other anchors, resistance may be mobilized in end bearing. Care must be taken to form and clean the underreams. (p. 8)
key_points: Tremie grouted holes with enlargement bells (p. 8).
Firm to hard cohesive deposits (p. 8).
End bearing added to side shear; form and clean underreams carefully (p. 8).

sections.title: Steel Bar and Strand Tendons
sections.summary: Bars (ASTM A722) of 26 to 64 mm in lengths up to about 18 m, a 64-mm bar resisting design loads up to about 2,077 kN, couplers beyond; easier to stress and adjust. Strand tendons (ASTM A416; indented A886) of multiple 15-mm seven-wire strands have no practical load or length limit; strand couplers not for routine use.
sections.body: Bar and strand tendons are both common for soil and rock anchors on U.S. highways, specified by ASTM A722 and ASTM A416 respectively; indented strand by ASTM A886. Bars are commonly available in 26, 32, 36, 45 and 64 mm diameters in uncoupled lengths up to approximately 18 m; a single 64-mm bar can resist design loads up to approximately 2,077 kN; couplers extend bars beyond 18 m or where space limits length. Compared with strands, bars are easier to stress and their load can be adjusted after lock-off. Strand tendons (p. 9) comprise multiple seven-wire strands, commonly 15 mm in diameter, with no practical load or length limitations; tendon steels have low enough relaxation to minimize long-term load losses. Strand couplers exist but are rarely used, since strand tendons can be made in any length; they are not recommended for routine projects, the coupler diameter being much larger than the strand, but may repair damaged tendons, with corrosion protection at the coupler verified. (pp. 8 to 9)
key_points: Bars per ASTM A722; strands per ASTM A416; indented strand ASTM A886 (p. 8).
Bars 26 to 64 mm, uncoupled lengths up to about 18 m (p. 8).

sections.title: Spacers and Centralizers
sections.summary: Spacer/centralizer units at regular intervals (typically 3 m) along the bond zone give strand tendons 6 to 13 mm interstrand spacing and at least 13 mm outer grout cover; noncorrosive, free-flowing (Figure 5).
sections.body: Spacer/centralizer units are placed at regular intervals (e.g., typically 3 m) along the anchor bond zone. For strand tendons, spacers usually provide a minimum interstrand spacing of 6 to 13 mm and a minimum outer grout cover of 13 mm. Spacers and centralizers should be made of non-corrosive materials and permit free flow of grout. Figures 5 and 6 show cut away sections of a bar and a strand tendon. (p. 9)
key_points: Spacer/centralizers typically every 3 m along the bond zone (p. 9).
Interstrand spacing 6 to 13 mm; outer grout cover at least 13 mm (p. 9).
Non-corrosive and free-flowing for grout (Figure 5) (p. 9).

sections.title: Epoxy-Coated Bar and Epoxy-Coated Filled Strand
sections.summary: Epoxy-coated bar (AASHTO M284) and filled strand (supplement to ASTM A882), used more for dam tiedowns, add corrosion protection; unfilled coated strand is not recommended. Deduct the strand's own creep (PTI 1996) from measured creep in acceptance testing.
sections.body: Epoxy-coated bar (AASHTO M284) and epoxy-coated filled strand (supplement to ASTM A882), not used extensively for highways, are increasingly used for dam tiedowns; the coating adds a layer of corrosion protection in the unbonded and bond lengths compared with bare steel. In filled strand the center wire is also coated; unfilled epoxy-coated strand is not recommended, since water may enter the gaps around the center wire and cause corrosion. Unlike bare strand, creep deformations of the epoxy-coated filled strands themselves are relatively significant during testing, and must be deducted from total creep movement to measure bond zone movement reliably; estimates of their intrinsic creep are in PTI (1996). Figure 6 shows a cut away strand tendon. (p. 10)
key_points: Epoxy-coated bar (AASHTO M284) and filled strand (ASTM A882 supplement) (p. 10).
Unfilled epoxy-coated strand not recommended (p. 10).

sections.title: Other Anchor Types and Tendon Materials
sections.summary: Grade 60 and 75 grouted bars, helical, plate and mechanical rock anchors are also used, but the document's design and testing methods are for cement grouted anchors with high strength prestressing steel. FRP tendons are under research and not in current U.S. practice.
sections.body: Alternative anchor types and tendon materials used in the U.S. include Grade 60 and Grade 75 grouted steel bars, helical anchors, plate anchors and mechanical rock anchors. The design and testing methods in the document are for cement grouted anchors using high strength prestressing steels and may not be appropriate for these alternatives. Fiber reinforced plastic (FRP) prestressing tendons are being researched (e.g., Schmidt et al., 1994) (p. 11): high tensile strength, corrosion resistant and lightweight, but not used in current U.S. practice; fiberglass and stainless steel have been used experimentally, cost and/or construction concerns restricting their use. (pp. 10 to 11)
key_points: Alternatives: Grade 60/75 grouted bars, helical, plate and mechanical rock anchors (p. 10).

sections.title: Cement Grout
sections.summary: Anchor grout is typically neat cement grout (ASTM C150); sand-cement for large holes, pea gravel-sand-cement outside the encapsulation. A w/c ratio of 0.4 to 0.55 with Type I cement normally gives at least 21 MPa at stressing; admixtures rarely needed, plasticizers for heat or long pumping.
sections.body: Anchor grout for soil and rock anchors is typically a neat cement grout (no aggregate) conforming to ASTM C150; sand-cement grout may be used for large diameter holes, and pea gravel-sand-cement grout outside the tendon encapsulation. High speed mixers commonly ensure uniform mixing. A water/cement (w/c) ratio of 0.4 to 0.55 by weight with Type I cement normally provides a minimum compressive strength of 21 MPa at the time of stressing. Special additives may be needed to improve flow on some projects; admixtures are not typically required, but plasticizers may help at high temperatures and for long pumping distances. (p. 11)
key_points: Neat cement grout per ASTM C150; sand-cement for large holes (p. 11).
w/c 0.4 to 0.55 with Type I cement: at least 21 MPa at stressing (p. 11).
Admixtures not typically required; plasticizers for heat or long pumping (p. 11).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Anchored walls are nongravity cantilevered walls with one or more anchor levels, using discrete (soldier beam) or continuous (sheet-pile) elements driven or drilled below grade; support from element stiffness, passive resistance and anchors. Facings usually CIP concrete; continuous elements need none.
sections.body: Anchored walls stabilizing excavations and slopes are a common highway application of ground anchors. They are nongravity cantilevered walls with one or more levels of anchors, using discrete (e.g., soldier beam) or continuous (e.g., sheet-pile) vertical elements driven or drilled below the finished excavation grade; nongravity cantilevered walls are supported by the shear and bending stiffness of the vertical elements and passive resistance below grade, and anchored walls add the lateral resistance of the anchors against horizontal pressures (earth, water, seismic). Discrete elements are often steel piles or drilled shafts spanned by a structural facing, permanent facings usually cast-in-place (CIP) concrete, though timber lagging or precast panels have been used. Continuous elements need no separate facing: steel sheet-piles, CIP or precast panels in slurry trenches (slurry or diaphragm walls), tangent/secant piles, soil-cement columns and jet grouted columns. (p. 11)
key_points: Nongravity cantilevered walls with one or more anchor levels (p. 11).
Discrete (soldier beam) or continuous (sheet-pile) elements (p. 11).
Support: element stiffness, passive resistance and anchors (p. 11).
Permanent facings usually CIP concrete; continuous walls need no facing (p. 11).

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Soldier beam and lagging walls, the most common U.S. anchored walls, span discrete elements with timber lagging or reinforced shotcrete; buildable in most ground but limited stand-up time in cohesionless soils and soft clays needs care; highly pervious (Figure 7).
sections.body: Soldier beam and lagging walls are the most commonly used anchored wall system in the U.S.: discrete vertical elements spanned by lagging, typically timber but possibly reinforced shotcrete. They can be built in most ground, but care is needed in ground such as cohesionless soils and soft clays with limited "stand-up" time for lagging installation; they are highly pervious. The construction sequence for a permanent wall is shown in Figure 7. (p. 12)
key_points: Most common U.S. anchored wall system (p. 12).
Timber lagging or reinforced shotcrete between discrete elements (p. 12).
Limited stand-up time in cohesionless soils and soft clays (p. 12).

sections.title: Soldier Beam
sections.summary: Soldier beams at 1.5 to 3 m: drilled-in steel sections backfilled with structural or lean-mix concrete to subgrade and lean-mix (about 1 MPa; specify at least 0.35 MPa, or CLSM) above; or driven HP or sheet sections with thru-beam connections or wales. Sidewinder connections and exposed wales are not for permanent walls.
sections.body: Soldier beams are installed from the ground surface to final elevation first, horizontal spacing typically 1.5 to 3 m; they may be steel beams or drilled shafts, the latter seldom with timber lagging. Drilled-in soldier beams: wide flange (WF) or double channel sections in holes backfilled with structural or lean-mix concrete from the bottom to excavation subgrade, chosen for the lateral and vertical capacity of the embedded part (chapter 5), and lean-mix from subgrade to surface, scraped off during lagging and anchor installation (structural concrete there is extremely hard to remove). Lean-mix typically has one 94 lb bag of Portland cement per cubic yard and strength not typically above about 1 MPa; controlled low strength material (CLSM, "flowable fill", with fine aggregate and fly ash) is an alternative; specifications should require a minimum strength of 0.35 MPa while keeping it easy to remove. Anchors are installed between the sections, the spacing set by the anchor type; hole diameters depend on the shape and anchor diameter; replacement anchors can go anywhere along the beam; connections on the front face or between sections, prefabricated for small diameter anchors, made after installation for large ones. Driven soldier beams: HP shapes or sheet piles, which must reach the embedment without significant damage, helped by drive shoes or "points" and high strength steel; if they cannot, they should be drilled-in. Thru-beam connections or horizontal wales connect the anchors. A thru-beam connection (p. 14), cut in the beam before driving for a small diameter anchor, applies the load at the beam center in line with the web; it cannot take large-diameter anchors (over about 150 mm) and suits projects with few expected anchor failures, since a failed anchor must be removed or a new connection made. A "sidewinder connection", offset from center and loading the flange, subjects the beam to bending and torsion; usable with a replacement anchor in a temporary support of excavation wall, it is not recommended for permanent walls. Wales may be on the face or recessed behind the front flange; exposed wales need well protected anchorages, are unattractive and corrode, and are not recommended for permanent walls; front-face wales need a thick CIP facing, recessed wales allow a normal facing but need costly individual fabrication and welding. If a wale is added during construction, check the horizontal clear distance to the travel lanes. (pp. 13 to 14)
key_points: Horizontal spacing typically 1.5 to 3 m (p. 13).
Drilled-in: structural or lean-mix concrete to subgrade, lean-mix above (p. 13).
Lean-mix about 1 MPa; specify at least 0.35 MPa for lean-mix or CLSM (p. 13).
Driven: HP or sheet sections; drill in if they cannot reach depth (p. 13).
Thru-beam connections not for anchors over about 150 mm (p. 14).
Sidewinder connections and exposed wales not recommended for permanent walls (p. 14).

sections.title: Lagging
sections.summary: Excavate in 1.2 to 1.5 m lifts (less with short stand-up time) and place lagging top-down promptly, behind or on the flanges, backpacked; louvers leave drainage gaps between boards, otherwise provide other drainage. Concrete lagging is problematic (tolerances, no trimming, cracking at anchors).
sections.body: After soldier beam installation the soil in front is excavated in lifts, commonly 1.2 to 1.5 m, smaller where stand-up time is limited, and lagging is placed top-down as soon as possible to limit erosion into the excavation, after trimming a reasonably smooth contact surface. Lagging behind the front flange is cut to length, placed between adjacent flanges and secured against the webs with wood wedges or shims; it can also be attached to the front flange with clips or welded studs, rarely behind the back flange. Gaps between lagging and retained ground must be backpacked for good contact. A spacer ("louver") nailed to the top of each board end leaves a drainage gap between vertically adjacent boards, wide enough to drain without letting soil fall out; boards in close contact are typically unacceptable, but where waterproofing requires no gap the contractor must provide alternate drainage. Concrete lagging (p. 15) is problematic: difficult handling, very tight tolerances on beam position for standard lengths, very difficult trimming, no field splicing, and possible cracking near anchors during testing or stressing. (pp. 14 to 15)
key_points: Excavate in 1.2 to 1.5 m lifts; smaller with limited stand-up time (p. 14).
Place lagging top-down as soon as possible; backpack gaps (p. 14).
Louvers leave drainage gaps; otherwise contractor provides drainage (p. 14).
Concrete lagging problematic (p. 15).

sections.title: Construction Sequence
sections.summary: Excavate to about 0.6 m below each anchor level (deeper only if the wall is designed for it), install, test and lock off the anchor, and repeat to final depth; then drainage elements and, for permanent walls, a precast or CIP facing. Shotcrete facing needs drainage behind it.
sections.body: Top-down lagging continues until the excavation is about 0.6 m below the design elevation of an anchor; excavation then stops and the anchor is installed. Deeper excavation (more than 0.6 m) below an anchor level may be needed to fabricate the connection or for equipment access, and the wall must be designed for it. The anchor is drilled and grouted, load tested once the grout has an appropriate minimum strength, and locked off at an appropriate load; excavation and lagging continue to the next anchor level, the cycle repeating to final depth. Prefabricated drainage elements may then be placed at design spacings and connected to a collector at the wall base. Shotcrete instead of timber lagging can be effective, but being of low permeability it needs drainage behind it (chapter 5). Permanent walls typically get a precast or CIP concrete facing. (p. 15)
key_points: Excavate about 0.6 m below each anchor level before installing it (p. 15).
Design the wall for any deeper excavation (p. 15).
Test and lock off each anchor before excavating further (p. 15).
Shotcrete needs drainage behind it; permanent walls get a precast or CIP facing (p. 15).

sections.title: Continuous Walls
sections.summary: Anchored continuous walls (sheet-pile, tangent or secant pile, slurry, soil mixed) are common for temporary support; sheet piles are driven in one phase, may be infeasible in hard ground or obstructions, and are normally steel. Continuous walls must be designed for water pressure, with watertight connections against permanent hydrostatic forces.
sections.body: Ground anchors are also used with continuous walls such as sheet-pile, tangent or secant pile, slurry or soil mixed walls, commonly for temporary excavation support. Sheet-pile walls are built in one phase, interlocking sheets driven to final elevation, often with a template in difficult driving, but may not be feasible in hard ground or with obstructions; steel sheets are normally used, being more available and stronger than precast concrete. Other continuous wall construction is covered in FHWA-HI-99-007 (1999). Continuous walls act as both vertical and horizontal elements; excavation and anchor installation cycle from the top and between anchor levels. Water pressure behind them must be considered in design, and where they resist permanent hydrostatic forces the anchor/wall connection must be watertight. (p. 15)
key_points: Continuous walls common for temporary excavation support (p. 15).
Sheet piles may be infeasible in hard ground or with obstructions; normally steel (p. 15).
Other continuous walls: FHWA-HI-99-007 (1999) (p. 15).
Design for water pressure; watertight connections against permanent hydrostatic forces (p. 15).

sections.summary: Heading for applications of ground anchors: highway retaining walls (2.4.1), slope and landslide stabilization (2.4.2) and tiedown structures (2.4.3).

sections.title: Highway Retaining Walls
sections.summary: Anchored walls serve depressed roadways, widenings and realignments, and bridge abutment construction or end slope removal; a gravity wall costs more because it needs temporary support, select backfill and possibly deep foundations (Figure 8).
sections.body: Anchored walls are commonly used for grade separations to build depressed roadways, roadway widenings and realignments; their advantages over conventional concrete gravity walls are described in "section 1.2" (as printed; the list is in 1.3). Figure 8 compares a gravity wall and a permanent anchored wall for a depressed roadway: the gravity wall is more expensive because it requires temporary excavation support, select backfill and possibly deep foundation support. Anchored walls may also be used for new bridge abutments and end slope removal at existing abutments (FHWA-RD-97-130, 1998). (p. 16)
key_points: Depressed roadways, widenings, realignments (p. 16).
Gravity wall costs more: temporary support, select backfill, deep foundations (Figure 8) (p. 16).
Also new abutments and end slope removal (FHWA-RD-97-130) (p. 16).

sections.title: Slope and Landslide Stabilization
sections.summary: Anchors with walls, beams or blocks permit deep cuts (Figure 9a) and stabilize landslides (Figure 9b) with forces possibly much larger than for a highway wall; beams or blocks need ground that does not run or compress at the face.
sections.body: Ground anchors are often combined with walls, horizontal beams or concrete blocks to stabilize slopes and landslides. Soil and rock anchors permit relatively deep cuts for new highways (Figure 9a) and can provide a large enough force to stabilize the ground mass above a landslide or slip surface (Figure 9b), possibly considerably more than a typical highway retaining wall needs. Horizontal beams or blocks may transfer the anchor loads to the slope surface provided the ground does not "run" or compress and can resist the reactions at the face; cost, aesthetics and long-term maintenance of the exposed face affect the choice. (p. 17)
key_points: Anchors permit relatively deep cuts (Figure 9a) (p. 17).
Landslide stabilization forces may far exceed wall needs (Figure 9b) (p. 17).
Beams or blocks need ground that does not run or compress (p. 17).

sections.title: Tiedown Structures
sections.summary: Tiedown anchors resist hydrostatic or overturning uplift (Figure 9c), reducing slab concrete and excavation or dewatering, but anchor loads vary with settlement and heave, watertight connections are difficult and slab stresses vary. Rock anchor tiedowns also stabilize concrete dams (Figure 9d).
sections.body: Permanent ground anchors may resist vertical uplift from hydrostatic or overturning forces, e.g. underwater where the structure's dead weight is insufficient (Figure 9c). Advantages: (1) less slab concrete than a dead weight slab; (2) less excavation and/or dewatering. Disadvantages: (1) potentially large variations in anchor load from settlement and heave of the structure; (2) difficulty making watertight connections at the anchor-slab interface, particularly important for hydrostatic applications; and (3) variations in slab stresses. A major uplift slab with tiedowns was built for the Central Artery Project in Boston, Massachusetts (Druss, 1994). Although not a highway application, permanent rock anchor tiedowns may stabilize concrete dams (Figure 9d), whose upgrades for maximum flood and earthquake standards benefit from added resistance to overturning, sliding and earthquake loading. Figure 9 (p. 18) shows the applications. (pp. 17 to 18)
key_points: Tiedowns resist hydrostatic or overturning uplift (Figure 9c) (p. 17).
Advantages: less slab concrete, less excavation or dewatering (p. 17).
Disadvantages: load variation, watertight connections, slab stresses (p. 17).
Rock anchor tiedowns for concrete dams (Figure 9d) (p. 17).
